nodes.name: Replacing fractions by equivalents leaves a sum or difference unchanged
nodes.statement: Replacing each fraction in a sum or difference by an equivalent fraction does not change the value of the sum or difference, so a/b + c/d can be rewritten as a sum of two fractions with a common denominator.
nodes.assess: True or false: 2/3 + 5/4 = 8/12 + 15/12. True or false: 2/3 + 5/4 = 2/12 + 5/12. Say which rule decides it.

proposed_edges.rationale: The statement is about the value of a sum, which means the total from joining parts of the same whole.
The sum stays the same because each fraction is a number, and replacing a number by an equal number cannot change a sum or difference.
The statement rewrites a/b and c/d over a common denominator, which is done by the multiplication principle for equivalent fractions.
Deciding that 8/12 and 15/12 are equivalent to 2/3 and 5/4, and that 2/12 is not equivalent to 2/3, requires recognizing equivalent fractions.
Each replaced fraction must be the same amount of the same whole, which is why the total of the amounts does not change.
The statement also covers differences, which means the amount left after separating parts of the same whole.

nodes.name: Add fractions with unlike denominators
nodes.statement: Add a/b + c/d by rewriting both fractions over a common multiple n of b and d (b x d always works), then adding the numerators over n.
nodes.assess: Compute 5/6 + 3/8.
procedure: Find a common multiple n of the denominators b and d (b x d is always one).
Rewrite a/b as (a x (n/b))/n and c/d as (c x (n/d))/n.
Add the two numerators and write the sum over n.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step 2 computes the multiplier n/b and n/d, which are whole-number quotients of the common multiple by each denominator.
Step 1 finds a common multiple n of the two denominators b and d.
Step 3 adds the two numerators and keeps the shared denominator n, the like-denominator addition procedure.
The rewriting in step 2 is allowed because replacing each fraction by an equivalent one leaves the sum unchanged.
Step 2 rewrites a/b and c/d as (a x (n/b))/n and (c x (n/d))/n, which generates equivalent fractions with denominator n.

nodes.name: Subtract fractions with unlike denominators
nodes.statement: For a/b at least c/d, find a/b - c/d by rewriting both fractions over a common multiple n of b and d (b x d always works), then subtracting the numerators over n.
nodes.assess: Compute 7/9 - 1/6.
procedure: Find a common multiple n of the denominators b and d (b x d is always one).
Rewrite a/b as (a x (n/b))/n and c/d as (c x (n/d))/n.
Subtract the second numerator from the first and write the difference over n.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step 2 computes the multiplier n/b and n/d, which are whole-number quotients of the common multiple by each denominator.
Step 1 finds a common multiple n of the two denominators b and d.
The rewriting in step 2 is allowed because replacing each fraction by an equivalent one leaves the difference unchanged.
Step 2 rewrites a/b and c/d as (a x (n/b))/n and (c x (n/d))/n, which generates equivalent fractions with denominator n.
Step 3 subtracts the second numerator from the first over the shared denominator n, the like-denominator subtraction procedure.

nodes.name: Add mixed numbers with unlike denominators
nodes.statement: Add two mixed numbers whose fraction parts have unlike denominators by adding whole parts and fraction parts separately over a common denominator, regrouping when the fraction parts sum to 1 or more.
nodes.assess: Compute 2 3/4 + 1 5/6.
procedure: Rewrite the two fraction parts over a common multiple of their denominators.
Add the fraction parts, and add the whole-number parts.
If the fraction sum is 1 or more, write it as 1 plus a fraction less than 1 and add the 1 to the whole-number sum.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step 1 rewrites the fraction parts over a common multiple of their two denominators.
Step 1 rewrites the two fraction parts over a common multiple of their denominators, exactly as unlike-denominator addition does.
Rewriting the fraction parts over a common denominator is valid because equivalent replacement leaves the total unchanged.
Step 1 produces the equivalent fractions over the common denominator for each fraction part.
Steps 2 and 3 add whole parts and fraction parts separately and regroup a fraction sum of 1 or more, as in like-denominator mixed-number addition.

nodes.name: Subtract mixed numbers with unlike denominators
nodes.statement: Subtract a smaller mixed number from a larger one when the fraction parts have unlike denominators by rewriting the fraction parts over a common denominator, regrouping 1 from the whole part when the first fraction part is smaller, then subtracting parts separately.
nodes.assess: Compute 4 1/6 - 1 3/4.
procedure: Rewrite the two fraction parts over a common multiple n of their denominators.
If the first fraction part is less than the second, take 1 from the first whole part and add n/n to its fraction part.
Subtract the fraction parts, and subtract the whole-number parts.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step 1 rewrites the fraction parts over a common multiple n of their two denominators.
Rewriting the fraction parts over a common denominator is valid because equivalent replacement leaves the difference unchanged.
Step 2 asks whether the first fraction part is less than the second, decided by comparing numerators over the common denominator n.
Step 1 produces the equivalent fractions over n for each fraction part.
Steps 2 and 3 compare fraction parts, regroup 1 from the whole part as n/n, and subtract parts separately, as in like-denominator mixed-number subtraction.
Step 1 rewrites the two fraction parts over a common multiple n of their denominators, as unlike-denominator subtraction does.

nodes.name: Solve word problems adding fractions of the same whole
nodes.statement: A story combines two fractional amounts of the same whole, possibly with unlike denominators; the learner represents it with an equation or model and finds the total.
nodes.assess: Maria walked 2/3 mile to the park and then 3/4 mile to the store. How far did she walk in all?

proposed_edges.rationale: The story combines two fractional amounts of the same whole, which is the joining meaning of addition.
The statement says the amounts may have unlike denominators, and the total is found by adding them with this procedure.
Representing the story with an equation or model extends the story-to-equation skill already used with like denominators.
The statement requires both amounts to be fractions of the same whole before they can be added.

nodes.name: Solve word problems subtracting fractions of the same whole
nodes.statement: A story takes away or compares two fractional amounts of the same whole, possibly with unlike denominators; the learner represents it with an equation or model and finds the difference.
nodes.assess: A jug held 7/8 liter of juice. Leo poured out 1/3 liter. How much juice is left?

proposed_edges.rationale: Representing the story with an equation or model extends the story-to-equation skill already used with like denominators.
The statement requires both amounts to be fractions of the same whole before they can be subtracted.
The story takes away or compares two fractional amounts of the same whole, which is the separating meaning of subtraction.
The statement says the amounts may have unlike denominators, and the difference is found by subtracting them with this procedure.

nodes.name: Estimate a fraction sum with benchmarks and judge reasonableness
nodes.statement: Estimate a sum of fractions by replacing each addend with a nearby benchmark (0, 1/2, 1, or a whole number), and use the estimate to judge whether a computed sum is reasonable.
nodes.assess: Without computing exactly, decide whether 2/5 + 1/2 = 3/7 can be correct, and explain using benchmark fractions.
procedure: Replace each addend with its nearest benchmark: 0, 1/2, 1, or a whole number.
Add the benchmarks to get an estimate of the sum.
Call a computed sum unreasonable if it is far from the estimate or is smaller than one of the addends.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step 2 adds benchmark whole numbers, for example 1 + 1, to produce the estimate.
Step 3 calls a sum unreasonable if it is smaller than an addend, because joining parts never gives less than one of the parts.
Step 2 adds benchmark fractions such as 1/2 + 1/2, which is like-denominator addition with a model.
Step 1 picks the nearest benchmark for each addend by reasoning about whether it is close to 0, 1/2, or 1.

nodes.name: Estimate a fraction difference with benchmarks and judge reasonableness
nodes.statement: Estimate a difference of fractions by replacing each fraction with a nearby benchmark (0, 1/2, 1, or a whole number), and use the estimate to judge whether a computed difference is reasonable.
nodes.assess: Jo says 11/12 - 3/8 = 8/4. Use benchmark fractions to decide whether this is reasonable.
procedure: Replace each fraction with its nearest benchmark: 0, 1/2, 1, or a whole number.
Subtract the benchmarks to get an estimate of the difference.
Call a computed difference unreasonable if it is far from the estimate or is larger than the first fraction.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step 1 picks the nearest benchmark for each fraction by reasoning about whether it is close to 0, 1/2, or 1.
Step 2 subtracts benchmark fractions such as 1 - 1/2, which is like-denominator subtraction with a model.
Step 3 calls a difference unreasonable if it is larger than the first fraction, because separating a part leaves no more than the whole amount.
Step 2 subtracts benchmark whole numbers, for example 2 - 1, to produce the estimate.

nodes.name: Find the two whole numbers a fraction lies between
nodes.statement: For a fraction a/b, divide a by b with remainder to get quotient q and remainder r; if r = 0 then a/b equals the whole number q, otherwise a/b lies strictly between q and q + 1.
nodes.assess: Between which two whole numbers does 47/6 lie?
procedure: Divide a by b to get a whole-number quotient q and remainder r.
If r = 0, a/b equals the whole number q.
Otherwise, a/b lies between the whole numbers q and q + 1.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step 1 divides a by b with a remainder to get the quotient q and remainder r.
Showing a/b lies below q + 1 uses r/b < b/b = 1, a comparison of two fractions with the same denominator.
Step 3 reads a/b as q plus the fraction r/b less than 1, so it lies between q and q + 1.
The fraction a/b is a copies of 1/b, and every b copies make one whole, which is why a/b contains q whole numbers.
Step 2 concludes that a/b equals the whole number q when r = 0, which treats q as a fraction with denominator 1.

nodes.name: A fraction as the share when a wholes are shared among b
nodes.statement: When a equal wholes are shared equally among b people, each person's share is a/b of one whole.
nodes.assess: 3 pizzas are shared equally among 4 people. Use a drawing to show how much pizza each person gets.

proposed_edges.rationale: The statement defines each person's share as the size of one equal share when a wholes are shared among b.
Each share is a parts of size 1/b, which is a non-unit fraction a/b of one whole.
The drawing of 3 pizzas shared by 4 cuts each pizza into 4 equal parts, each a unit fraction 1/4 of a pizza.
Showing the sharing of 3 pizzas among 4 people requires drawing and cutting wholes into equal shares.

nodes.name: a divided by b equals a/b
nodes.statement: For whole numbers a and b with b greater than 0, a divided by b equals the fraction a/b.
nodes.assess: Write 7 divided by 3 as a fraction. Write 5/8 as a division of two whole numbers.

proposed_edges.rationale: The statement uses a divided by b, meaning the size of each of b equal shares of a.
Writing a sharing situation as a divided by b is the division expression whose value the statement names a/b.
a divided by b is the number that multiplied by b gives a, the unknown-factor meaning of the quotient.
Checking that b x (a/b) = (b x a)/b = a shows a/b is the unknown factor, which uses n x (a/b) = (n x a)/b.
Sharing a wholes among b gives each a/b, which is why a divided by b equals the fraction a/b.

nodes.name: Solve division word problems with fraction or mixed-number answers
nodes.statement: A story divides a whole number of units equally into a whole number of shares where the answer is not a whole number; the learner writes the quotient as a fraction or mixed number.
nodes.assess: 9 people share a 50-pound sack of rice equally by weight. How many pounds does each person get, and between what two whole numbers does the answer lie?

proposed_edges.rationale: The learner first models the equal-sharing story and writes the division expression such as 50 divided by 9.
The test question asks between what two whole numbers the answer lies.
The statement allows a mixed-number answer, which is a whole number plus a fraction.
Writing the non-whole quotient as a fraction uses a divided by b equals a/b.

nodes.name: (a/b) x q as a parts of q split into b equal parts, q whole
nodes.statement: For a whole number q, (a/b) x q is the amount formed by a parts when q is partitioned into b equal parts.
nodes.assess: Use a drawing to show (2/3) x 4 as parts of 4 split into 3 equal parts. What is the product?

proposed_edges.rationale: Partitioning q into b equal parts is the sharing meaning of division, with each part the size of one share.
Finding the product of (2/3) x 4 from a drawing requires combining the equal parts into a total with unit fractions.
The product is formed by a parts of the equal parts, each of size 1/b of the partitioned quantity.
When q is not a multiple of b, each of the b equal parts of q is itself a fraction of a whole.

nodes.name: (a/b) x (c/d) as a parts of c/d split into b equal parts
nodes.statement: For a fraction c/d, (a/b) x (c/d) is the amount formed by a parts when c/d is partitioned into b equal parts.
nodes.assess: Use a fraction model to show (2/3) x (4/5) as parts of 4/5 split into 3 equal parts. What is the product?

proposed_edges.rationale: Splitting c/d into b equal parts splits each unit fraction 1/d into b smaller parts, as in sharing a unit fraction.
The statement is the same partition-and-take-a-parts meaning, now applied to a fraction c/d in place of a whole number q.
Taking 2 parts of size 4/15 to read the product 8/15 is a whole number times a fraction.
The quantity c/d being partitioned is itself c parts of size 1/d of a whole.
Partitioning the amount c/d into b equal parts means splitting a shaded region of a model into equal-area parts.

nodes.name: (a/b) x q equals a x q divided by b
nodes.statement: For any whole number or fraction q, (a/b) x q equals the result of multiplying q by a and then dividing by b.
nodes.assess: Write (2/3) x 4 as a multiplication followed by a division, and find the result.

proposed_edges.rationale: The same a-of-b-equal-parts reasoning supports the statement when q is a fraction.
Taking a of the b equal parts of a whole number q is a groups of q divided by b, which equals a x q divided by b.
Writing the result of 8 divided by 3 as the fraction 8/3 is needed to state the product in the test problem.
Showing a x (q divided by b) equals (a x q) divided by b uses associativity and commutativity of multiplication.

nodes.name: The product rule (a/b) x (c/d) = (a x c)/(b x d)
nodes.statement: For any fractions a/b and c/d, (a/b) x (c/d) = (a x c)/(b x d), where a whole number q is written as q/1.
nodes.assess: True or false: (2/3) x (4/5) = 8/15. True or false: (2/3) x (4/5) = 6/8. Say which rule decides it.

proposed_edges.rationale: Dividing (a x c)/d by b gives (a x c)/(d x b), which rests on the rule (1/d) divided by b = 1/(d x b).
Writing (a/b) x (c/d) as a x (c/d) divided by b is the first step of deriving the product rule.
The product (a/b) x (c/d) is first defined as a parts of c/d split into b equal parts, which the rule then computes.
The step a x (c/d) = (a x c)/d is the whole-number-times-fraction rule.
The statement writes a whole number q as q/1 so that the rule also covers whole-number factors.
The area model shows the product as a x c small rectangles, each 1/(b x d) of the unit square, which is the rule.

nodes.name: Multiply a fraction or whole number by a fraction
nodes.statement: Multiply a fraction or whole number by a fraction by multiplying numerators and multiplying denominators, after writing any whole number q as q/1.
nodes.assess: Compute (3/4) x (5/6) and (2/9) x 6.
procedure: Write any whole-number factor q as q/1.
Multiply the numerators to get the numerator of the product.
Multiply the denominators to get the denominator of the product.

proposed_edges.rationale: Steps 2 and 3 multiply numerators and denominators, which is carrying out the product rule.
Step 1 writes a whole-number factor q as the fraction q/1.
Multiplying the numerators and the denominators are whole-number multiplications that may involve several digits.

nodes.name: Multiply mixed numbers
nodes.statement: Multiply mixed numbers by rewriting each as a fraction, multiplying with the product rule, and rewriting the result as a mixed number if wanted.
nodes.assess: Compute 2 1/2 x 1 1/3.
procedure: Rewrite each mixed number w a/b as the fraction (w x b + a)/b.
Multiply the fractions: multiply numerators and multiply denominators.
If the product is 1 or more, divide numerator by denominator to write it as a mixed number.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step 3 divides the numerator by the denominator to get a whole-number quotient and remainder.
Step 3 divides numerator by denominator to find the whole part and remainder of the mixed-number answer.
The product 20/6 of the test problem must be reduced to 3 1/3, which requires recognizing 2/6 equals 1/3.
Writing the product as a quotient plus remainder over the denominator uses the meaning of a mixed number.
Step 1 rewrites each mixed number w a/b as the fraction (w x b + a)/b.
Step 2 multiplies the two fractions by multiplying numerators and multiplying denominators.

nodes.name: Find the area of a fraction-sided rectangle by tiling with unit-fraction squares
nodes.statement: Find the area of a rectangle with fractional side lengths by rewriting both sides over a common denominator n, tiling the rectangle with squares of side 1/n, and counting squares, each of area 1/(n x n).
nodes.assess: A rectangle is 3/4 m by 1/2 m. Tile it with squares of side 1/4 m and find its area.
procedure: Rewrite both side lengths over a common denominator n, as p/n and q/n.
Tile the rectangle with squares of side 1/n: p along one side and q along the other.
Note that n x n such squares fill a unit square, so each has area 1/(n x n).
Count the p x q squares; the area is (p x q)/(n x n) square units.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step 4 counts the p x q squares in the rectangle as rows times columns, as in finding area by tiling.
Step 1 needs a common denominator n for the two side lengths, found as a common multiple of the denominators.
Step 1 rewrites each side length as an equivalent fraction p/n or q/n.
Step 1 rewrites each side length as an equivalent fraction over n, such as 1/2 as 2/4.
Step 2 uses that a side of length p/n is p copies of the unit fraction 1/n, so p squares fit along it.
Step 2 lays p squares along a side of length p/n, because p/n is a sum of p unit fractions 1/n.
Step 3 shows each small square is one of n x n equal parts of the unit square, so its area is 1/(n x n).

nodes.name: Find the area of a fraction-sided rectangle by multiplying side lengths
nodes.statement: The area of a rectangle with side lengths a/b and c/d is found by computing (a/b) x (c/d) with the product rule.
nodes.assess: Find the area of a rectangle that is 3/5 m by 2/3 m.
procedure: Multiply the two side lengths with the product rule (a x c)/(b x d).
Label the result in square units.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step 2 labels the result in square units, using area as side length times side length.
Step 1 multiplies the two side lengths using the product rule on fractions.
Tiling with unit-fraction squares is how the area of a fraction-sided rectangle was first found, and the product must match it.

nodes.name: Represent a fraction product as a rectangular area
nodes.statement: The product (a/b) x (c/d) is shown as the area of an a/b-by-c/d rectangle drawn inside a unit square whose sides are partitioned into b and d equal parts.
nodes.assess: Draw an area model for (2/3) x (3/4) and use it to name the product.
procedure: Draw a unit square.
Partition one side into b equal parts and the other side into d equal parts, making b x d small rectangles.
Shade the rectangle that is a parts by c parts; it holds a x c small rectangles, so its area is (a x c)/(b x d).

proposed_edges.rationale: Step 3 counts the a x c small rectangles in the shaded array, as rows times columns.
The product (a/b) x (c/d) being drawn is defined as a parts of c/d split into b equal parts.
Step 3 shades a of the b parts along one side and c of the d parts along the other.
Each small rectangle is one of the b x d equal parts of the unit square, so its area is 1/(b x d).
Step 2 partitions the sides of the unit square into b and d equal parts.

nodes.name: Explain why tiling and multiplying give the same area
nodes.statement: With both sides written as p/n and q/n, tiling gives p x q squares of area 1/(n x n), an area of (p x q)/(n x n), which is exactly (p/n) x (q/n) by the product rule; so for any fractional side lengths the two methods agree.
nodes.assess: Explain why tiling a 2/3-by-4/5 rectangle with small squares gives the same area as computing (2/3) x (4/5), and why the same argument works for any fractional side lengths.

proposed_edges.rationale: The argument for any side lengths relies on rewriting both fractions over a common denominator n by the multiplication principle.
The explanation shows (p x q)/(n x n) is exactly (p/n) x (q/n) by the product rule.
The statement compares the tiling area with the area found by multiplying side lengths.
The explanation uses the tiling count of p x q squares each of area 1/(n x n).

nodes.name: Multiplication as resizing
nodes.statement: Multiplying a quantity by a factor resizes the quantity: the product is the quantity stretched or shrunk by that factor.
nodes.assess: A picture 6 inches wide is resized by a factor of 3/2. Is the new picture wider or narrower, and how wide is it?

proposed_edges.rationale: Deciding whether the picture is wider or narrower requires reasoning about whether 3/2 is more or less than 1.
Resizing by a fraction factor such as 3/2 takes a parts of b equal parts of the quantity.
Stretching by a whole-number factor is the 'n times as much' comparison.

nodes.name: The scaling size principle
nodes.statement: For a positive number q and a positive factor f, q x f is greater than q when f > 1, equal to q when f = 1, and less than q when f < 1.
nodes.assess: True or false: (3/5) x 48 is greater than 48. True or false: (7/4) x 48 is greater than 48. Say which rule decides it.

proposed_edges.rationale: The three cases depend on comparing the factor f with the benchmark 1.
The case f = 1 uses that multiplying by 1 leaves the number unchanged.
The principle says whether resizing by factor f stretches or shrinks the quantity q.

nodes.name: Compare a product with a factor without multiplying
nodes.statement: Decide whether a product of positive numbers is greater than, equal to, or less than one factor by comparing the other factor with 1, without performing the multiplication.
nodes.assess: Without multiplying, put these in order from least to greatest: 225, (9/10) x 225, (11/8) x 225.
procedure: Pick the factor q to compare the product with; call the other factor f.
Compare f with 1.
Conclude: the product is greater than q if f > 1, equal to q if f = 1, and less than q if f < 1.

proposed_edges.rationale: Putting the three products in order and recording the order requires comparing numbers with symbols.
Step 2 compares the factor f with 1, which is comparing a fraction with a benchmark.
Step 1 may pick either factor as the one to compare against, which uses the commutative property of multiplication.
Step 3 concludes greater, equal, or less using the scaling size principle.

nodes.name: Explain why multiplying by a fraction greater than 1 makes a number larger
nodes.statement: For a positive number q and a fraction f > 1, write f = 1 + g with g > 0; then q x f = q + q x g, which is q plus a positive amount, so q x f > q. Multiplying by a whole number greater than 1 is the familiar case.
nodes.assess: Explain why (5/4) x 12 is greater than 12, and why the same reasoning works for any fraction greater than 1.

proposed_edges.rationale: Adding the positive amount q x g to q gives a total larger than q.
Writing f = 1 + g for a fraction f > 1 decomposes the fraction as b/b plus a fraction with the same denominator.
Writing f = 1 + g with g > 0 treats f as a whole number plus a fraction.
Seeing that q x g is a positive amount uses the product of two positive fractions having positive numerator and denominator.
The step q x 1 = q uses that multiplying by 1 leaves a number unchanged.
The step q x (1 + g) = q x 1 + q x g is the distributive property.
The explanation justifies the claim that q x f is greater than q when f is greater than 1.

nodes.name: Explain why multiplying by a fraction less than 1 makes a number smaller
nodes.statement: For a positive number q and a fraction a/b with 0 < a < b, (a/b) x q is a of the b equal parts of q, fewer than all b parts, so (a/b) x q < q.
nodes.assess: Explain why (3/4) x 12 is less than 12, and why the same reasoning works for any positive fraction less than 1.

proposed_edges.rationale: The same argument is meant to work when the positive number q is a fraction.
The argument reads (a/b) x q as a of the b equal parts of a whole number q.
The explanation justifies the claim that q x f is less than q when f is less than 1.
Taking fewer than all b parts gives less than q because q itself is all b of its equal parts.

nodes.name: Relate a/b = (n x a)/(n x b) to multiplying by 1
nodes.statement: Since (n x a)/(n x b) = (n/n) x (a/b) and n/n = 1, the equivalence principle a/b = (n x a)/(n x b) says that multiplying a/b by 1 does not change it.
nodes.assess: Explain how the equation 2/3 = (5 x 2)/(5 x 3) is an example of multiplying 2/3 by 1.

proposed_edges.rationale: The statement restates the equivalence principle a/b = (n x a)/(n x b) as multiplication by 1.
Writing (n x a)/(n x b) as (n/n) x (a/b) is the product rule read backward.
The step n/n = 1 treats the whole number 1 as the fraction n/n.
The conclusion uses that multiplying a/b by 1 does not change it.

nodes.name: Solve real-world fraction multiplication problems with a visual model
nodes.statement: A real-world problem asks for a fraction of a fractional or mixed-number quantity; the learner represents it with a visual fraction model and reads the answer from the model.
nodes.assess: A garden is 3/4 of an acre. 2/3 of the garden is planted with corn. Draw a model to find how many acres are planted with corn.

proposed_edges.rationale: Drawing a visual model for a story extends the model-drawing skill used with a fraction times a whole number.
The statement allows a mixed-number quantity, which is a whole number plus a fraction in the model.
Finding a fraction of a fractional quantity in a model means taking a parts of the quantity split into b equal parts.
The visual model for the product is the area model of a fraction times a fraction.

nodes.name: Solve real-world fraction multiplication problems with an equation
nodes.statement: A real-world problem asks for a fraction or mixed-number multiple of a quantity; the learner writes a multiplication equation and solves it symbolically.
nodes.assess: A recipe uses 2 1/4 cups of flour. How much flour is needed for 1 1/2 batches? Write an equation and solve it.

proposed_edges.rationale: Writing the multiplication equation for a story extends writing an equation for a fraction-times-whole-number problem.
The statement allows mixed-number multiples, such as 1 1/2 batches of 2 1/4 cups.
The phrase a fraction of a quantity must be recognized as multiplication by that fraction to write the equation.
The learner solves the equation symbolically by multiplying numerators and denominators.

nodes.name: (1/b) divided by n as sharing 1/b into n equal parts
nodes.statement: (1/b) divided by n is the size of each part when 1/b is partitioned into n equal parts; splitting each of the whole's b parts into n makes b x n equal parts, so each share is 1/(b x n) of the whole.
nodes.assess: Draw a fraction model to show 1/3 divided by 4, and tell a story the division could describe.

proposed_edges.rationale: The division is the size of each part when 1/b is partitioned into n equal parts.
Each share is one of the b x n equal parts of the whole, which is the unit fraction 1/(b x n).
Splitting each of the b parts into n makes b groups of n equal parts, so b x n parts in all.
Splitting each of the whole's b parts into n equal-area parts is how the model is drawn.
Drawing a model of 1/3 divided by 4 requires cutting a shape into equal shares and cutting those again.

nodes.name: (1/b) divided by n = 1/(b x n)
nodes.statement: For whole numbers b and n greater than 0, (1/b) divided by n = 1/(b x n).
nodes.assess: True or false: 1/5 divided by 2 = 1/10. True or false: 1/5 divided by 2 = 2/5. Say which rule decides it.

proposed_edges.rationale: The rule states the size of each part found when 1/b is shared into n equal parts.

nodes.name: Divide a unit fraction by a whole number
nodes.statement: Compute (1/b) divided by a whole number n greater than 0 by multiplying the denominator b by n.
nodes.assess: Compute 1/4 divided by 3.
procedure: Multiply the denominator b by the divisor n.
Write the quotient as 1/(b x n).

proposed_edges.rationale: Steps 1 and 2 apply the rule (1/b) divided by n = 1/(b x n).
Step 1 multiplies the denominator b by the divisor n, which may be multi-digit.

nodes.name: Explain (1/b) divided by n = 1/(b x n) with multiplication
